original_value: Electrical and optical biointerfaces have contributed considerably to understanding biological systems. Recent advances in biocompatible materials, structure designs, and fabrication techniques have established flexible and minimally invasive electronic/optoelectronic platforms that laminate onto targeted surface regions or implant into precise locations of biosystems to monitor and control various biological processes at cell, tissue, and organ levels. Herein, recent progress in advanced biointegrated electrical and optical platforms is discussed. An overview of materials and device designs to form flexible and even stretchable electrodes is presented. Strategies to reduce tissue damage and foreign‐body response to improve chronic stability are described. State‐of‐the‐art wearable and implantable microsystems with/without wireless capabilities for bioelectrical sensing and stimulation, optical recording and modulation, and multimodal operation are highlighted. In conclusion, a discussion of the remaining obstacles for future research in these areas is provided.

result.paraphrase: Electrical and optical biointerfaces have played a major role in advancing understanding of biological systems. Recent progress in biocompatible materials, structural design, and fabrication methods has enabled flexible, minimally invasive electronic/optoelectronic platforms that can laminate onto selected surface regions or be implanted at precise sites in biosystems to monitor and control biological processes at the cellular, tissue, and organ scales. This review surveys recent advances in biointegrated electrical and optical platforms. It outlines materials and device designs used to create flexible and even stretchable electrodes, describes approaches for minimizing tissue damage and foreign-body responses to enhance long-term stability, and highlights state-of-the-art wearable and implantable microsystems with or without wireless capability for bioelectrical sensing and stimulation, optical recording and modulation, and multimodal operation. Finally, it discusses the remaining challenges for future research in these areas.
